The Joyce Project is the work of John Hunt, who taught literature classes at the University of Montana in Missoula from 1988 to 2019. In the second half of his teaching career he offered classes in the works of James Joyce, with an emphasis on Ulysses, and he began to think that a website might offer students a single capacious way of accessing the information they need to make sense of this overwhelming novel, not as a mere supplemental resource but as part of the reading experience. His idea was to encode a complete text of the novel embedded with hyperlinks of different colors to take users to explanatory notes in various categories of interest. With the help of two graduate students he began work on the site in 2010, and as of 2026 he is still happily diving into the luminous obscurities of Joyce's text. Over time, his understanding of what the site could be has evolved, and others have suggested new kinds of functionality. The result has been longer and more exploratory notes, new "Resources," an alphabetical index of note titles, mobile access, an ebook for offline reading, and search capacity. The basic goals, however, have remained the same: immediate linkage from text to interpretive context; concise help for beginners and more involved discussion for experienced readers; tracing of the novel's endless nonlinear connections; variable pagination for users of different printed texts; and abundant visual illustrations. The Joyce Project currently contains nearly 1,200 notes. More will follow, for as long as forever is.


From the beginning, people with coding skills have worked with John to translate his conceptual and visual plans for the site into virtual reality. The original version, launched in January 2010, was developed by UM graduate student Tom Seiler, whose design enabled color coding, hyperlinks that could be turned on and off, and variable pagination. Over the course of the next two years graduate student Barb Nelson loaded the eighteen chapters of the novel onto this platform, starting with the Project Gutenberg electronic text. September 2012 saw the launch of a new site version with significantly improved graphic appearance and some added functionality, the coding work this time being executed by John's son Alex Hunt. In March 2016 Patrick Boe, a software engineer in Philadelphia, launched a separate site version (m.joyceproject.com) for smartphones and tablets. In March 2018 Andy Han contributed a more elegant way of encoding variable pagination. In January 2021 the desktop site added a downloadable ebook built around the Gutenberg epub file. Developed by Sahas Subramanian, a software engineer in Berlin, it includes an index to the notes and a preface for new readers of the novel.

March 2025 saw the release of a major new site version developed by Alex Hunt. This more powerful and stable website integrates mobile and desktop designs in a single responsive web design. It relieves the writer of notes from the headaches of working with HTML and Javascript and offers users a single way to search for appearances of text, whether in the notes, chapters of the novel, or explanatory pages. The new site uses a React Redux application built with Meta's Draft.js library on the front end, with Flask and Elasticsearch on the back end. The source code is freely available under the MIT license (github.com/alexchunt90/joyce) for anyone to adapt for their own hypertext annotation project. (Interest has been expressed in constructing a similar site for Finnegans Wake.) Thanks also are due to Alex for the many times over the years in which he has rescued his father when technical glitches threatened to interrupt progress.


Three Irishmen have regularly corresponded with John about the project, offering ideas for notes and responding to what he has written. Before his retirement, Dubliner Vincent Altman O’Connor pursued a career in the Department of Agriculture while playing blues and jazz piano on the side. He has consulted on many details of Hiberno-Hebraic coexistence, Fenian nationalism, Dublin psychotopography, and music. Dubliner Senan Molony is an alum of Joyce's Belvedere College and an award-winning journalist who has published ten books, including The Phoenix Park Murders and Helen of Joyce. Parts of the latter book and several of his unpublished papers and lectures on Ulysses are mentioned in notes, and he has communicated opinions on many topics ranging from Irish language to life in Dublin to literary allusions, as well as contributing some images. Derry resident Vincent Van Wyk grew up in South Africa and was educated at Ulster University. His recommendations for notes have ranged across topics as various as film, philosophy, the Boer War, sexual perversities, material culture, natural science, and Ulster people.


For many years the notes on the site received scrupulous and grammatically exacting proofreading from Ole Bønnerup, an Aarhus resident retired from teaching English and French in a Danish high school. Bønnerup's generous efforts extended to other demanding tasks like tracking textual variants in different editions of the novel, helping John with his ongoing effort to post the best possible online edition of a notoriously contested text.

Other people, listed here alphabetically, have written notes or contributed supplementary resources to the site:

Marco Fulvio Barozzi, a retired teacher of mathematics who honeymooned in Dublin and lives in Milan, co-authored a note on Almidano Artifoni.
Sean Collins, a UM graduate student who went on to doctoral work at the University of Utah, collaborated on a note on Montaigne's cat.
Andy Han, a Cincinnati high school student, wrote a note on shrewridden husbands.
Bruce Hardy, a pediatric cardiologist in Missoula who taught classes in Joyce's works after retirement, was lead author of a note on the death of Rudy Bloom.
Michael Kirkham, a lecturer at the University of Dundee, has contributed his jigsaw-puzzle image of Joyce's Dublin geography as a starting point for exploring Places in the Novel.
Morgan Lawrence, a UM undergraduate, co-wrote a note on aconite for a senior seminar.
Senan Molony, described above, wrote a note on "punched tickets" and has co-written notes on hirsute comets, the "writing on the wall," Meade's timberyard, and a French story of "mistaken identity."
Barb Nelson, a UM graduate student, compiled an exhaustive list of People in the Novel.
Doug Pope, a Nova Scotia artist and educator, wrote notes on advertising "puffs" and Stephen's telegram and co-wrote notes on Lord Byron and Molly's "Yes."
Russell Raphael, author of An Understanding of Ulysses and founder of the reading group North London Ulysses, collaborated on a note on Dante's Paradiso.
Josh Wagner, a novelist and playwright, wrote notes on Bloom's "floating flower" and Stephen's "I, I, and I" for a senior seminar as a UM undergraduate.

Many others (this list is certainly incomplete) have written to correct or amplify notes, propose ideas for new ones, contribute images, or point out oddities in the text:
